F6.quote: The rapid growth of generative AI including popular models such as ChatGPT, Microsoft’s Copilot and Google’s Gemini (formerly Bard) have brought to fore many new legal issues relating to ownership, subsistence and infringement of copyright law.
F6.claim: generative AI has raised new legal issues of ownership, subsistence and infringement of copyright
F6.lineage: the questions its cases turn on
F6.date: 2025-10-31 (the page's date, 31 Oct 2025; entries to 31 July 2026)

F7.quote: At the heart of the discourse is the reinterpretation of copyright principles in the age of AI-generated content.
F7.claim: the discourse turns on reinterpreting copyright principles for AI-generated content
F7.lineage: the questions its cases turn on
F7.date: 2025-10-31 (the page's date, 31 Oct 2025; entries to 31 July 2026)

F8.quote: It is unsurprising that the US Courts have led the way in AI & copyright litigation to date given most of the leading AI technology providers are based there, but we are starting to see similar claims being issued elsewhere including before UK and European Courts.
F8.claim: US courts have led AI and copyright litigation, the leading providers being based there; similar claims are beginning before UK and European courts
F8.lineage: the US claims: a sentence about the field
F8.date: 2025-10-31 (the page's date, 31 Oct 2025; entries to 31 July 2026)

F9.quote: Is there a valid infringement claim where the entirety of a copyright work is copied for the purpose of training a large language model but the “allegedly infringing” output seen by consumers only contains “infinitesimally small” reproductions of the original work, which is the case in UK case Getty Images (US) Inc & Ors v Stability AI Ltd?
F9.claim: a question UK and European courts face: infringement where a whole work is copied to train a large language model but outputs carry only infinitesimally small reproductions, the question of Getty v Stability AI
F9.lineage: the questions its cases turn on
F9.date: 2025-10-31 (the page's date, 31 Oct 2025; entries to 31 July 2026)

F10.quote: What about if the defendant argues the dataset used for training said machine is using only transient copies of the original work , which is the case in German case Robert Kneschke & LAION e.V.?
F10.claim: a question: transient copies in a training dataset, the question of Kneschke v LAION
F10.lineage: the questions its cases turn on
F10.date: 2025-10-31 (the page's date, 31 Oct 2025; entries to 31 July 2026)

F11.quote: And how do we define the authorship of work created by AI, particularly where the law may define the author as a “natural person” which is/has been considered in the Czech Republic between S. Š. (individual) v TAUBEL LEGAL, advokátní kancelář s.r.o. Case No. 13/2023?
F11.claim: a question: authorship of AI-created work where the law defines the author as a natural person, considered in the Czech case S. Š. v TAUBEL LEGAL
F11.lineage: the questions its cases turn on
F11.date: 2025-10-31 (the page's date, 31 Oct 2025; entries to 31 July 2026)

F12.quote: These are some of the issues emerging from the adoption and use of generative AI, an area that is likely to be increasingly complicated by newer and more advanced technologies, and the implementation of the EU AI Act.

F22.quote: On 24 July 2026, the DHC passed an interim order refusing ANI’s request for an interim injunction, holding that at the prima facie stage, OpenAI’s use of ANI’s content to train ChatGPT models falls under the ‘fair dealing’ exception under Section 52(1)(a)(i) of the Copyright Act.
F22.claim: the interim order of 24 July 2026: injunction refused; at the prima facie stage OpenAI's use of ANI's content to train ChatGPT models falls under the fair dealing exception of s.52(1)(a)(i)
F22.lineage: case: ANI Media v OpenAI (Delhi High Court)
F22.date: 2025-06-25 (the page's date, 25 Jun 2025; status as on 24 July 2026)

F23.claim: its limit: the ruling is interim and prima facie; the main suit continues on the merits
F23.lineage: case: ANI Media v OpenAI (Delhi High Court)
F23.date: 2025-06-25 (the page's date, 25 Jun 2025; status as on 24 July 2026)

F24.quote: formulated a three-factor assessment for the present case: (i) whether the use of ANI’s works was limited to LLM training; (ii) whether such use resulted in market competition or prejudice to ANI’s legitimate commercial interests; and (iii) whether ChatGPT’s functions served a broader public interest.
F24.claim: the court's three-factor fair dealing test: use limited to LLM training, market competition or prejudice, broader public interest
F24.lineage: case: ANI Media v OpenAI (Delhi High Court)
F24.date: 2025-06-25 (the page's date, 25 Jun 2025; status as on 24 July 2026)

F25.quote: held, prima facie, that the responses in question could not have resulted from memorisation of ANI’s works during training but rather using the RAG technique, through which LLMs retrieve relevant information from external sources.
